newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds mixed, focus on EMU fears.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds mixed, focus on EMU fears.

text.p: Irish bonds were mixed in thin trade on Monday, failing to find inspiration from the outcome of the Irish general election and dampened by a fresh bout of EMU uncertainty, dealers said.

"From the market's point of view the election outcome was not decisive enough," a dealer said. "It's only a marginally negative factor but it's there all the same. Also, the French kicking up about the stability pact has added to an already nervy EMU backdrop."
By 1505 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up 10 pence at 101.55 to yield 6.07 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was down 25 pence at 108.50 to yield 6.72 percent.
Dealers said they had seen investors keen to reduce risk selling 10-year paper to buy five-year bonds which also enjoyed a recovery from a sell-off on Friday.
Yields against German bunds had diverged from Friday's close to stand at 166 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 95 over in the 10-year, traders said.
On Monday, Fianna Fail leader Bertie Ahern began preparations to form a minority government after his alliance's narrow win in the weekend's cliff-hanger election.

The centre-right opposition of Fianna Fail and Progressive Democrat alliance fell two seats short of a majority, holding 81 out of 166 seats. They will need the backing of independents to control parliament.
Dealers said the lack of an overtly positive outcome meant the Irish bond market might not claw its way back from its underperformance last week.

Also on Monday, new French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told his EU counterparts that France was determined to see a single currency start in 1999 but that he wanted a period of reflection before signing the stability pact which sets out fines for countries not keeping their budget deficits in order.
That sparked immediate speculation about a delay for EMU or a fudging of the criteria.
Looking ahead, dealers said, Irish CPI figures due on Thursday should be supportive of the market.
On the international scene, U.S. retail sales and producer price data are due on Thursday and Friday and are likely to reignite interest rate speculation over there, and hence world-wide.
But for the early part of the week, European economic and monetary union will dominate.
